turns.user: What is the ONT receiver sensitivity?
turns.answer:
ONT receiver sensitivity isn't something this system models — it's deliberately not in the dataset or the optical constants, so I can't give you a figure for it.

What the system does instead: optical budgets here are computed against the GPON class budget, and links are classified as pass/marginal/fail against that plus the recommended minimum margin. Received power for a subscriber is reported only as an estimate, with no receiver sensitivity behind it — so the system also can't tell you whether a given ONT will work.

turns.user: How does cascaded splitter loss affect a link budget?
turns.answer:
From the documentation (splitters-and-cascades.md): 
a cascade is a splitter fed from the output of another splitter rather than directly from the OLT, and cascaded splitter loss is additive — the insertion loss of every splitter stage in the chain applies to every subscriber downstream of the last one, on top of the fiber, connector and splice loss the path already carries.



It's the single most common reason an otherwise reasonable-looking link ends up marginal or fails its budget outright: two cascaded splitters of a modest ratio can easily contribute more insertion loss than either ratio alone would suggest, because the losses of both stages stack rather than averaging. A review that only checks the final splitter's ratio, without walking the whole chain back to the OLT, will consistently under-estimate total splitter insertion loss.
 
So when a link is marginal, checking whether it descends from a cascade — and how many stages deep — is usually the fastest way to find where the loss came from.



Each doubling of the splitter ratio adds several decibels of insertion loss to every subscriber on it
. The per-ratio figures the system computes with (from its constants) are: 1:2 = 3.5 dB, 1:4 = 7.2 dB, 1:8 = 10.5 dB, 1:16 = 13.5 dB, 1:32 = 17 dB — all flagged industry-typical, pending validation.

The stacked total is then checked against the class budget — 
Class B+ allows 28 dB, Class C+ allows 32 dB
 — with a recommended minimum margin of 3 dB in this project's constants. 
A link sitting right at its class limit has no room for degradation.


If you want, I can run the per-hop breakdown for a specific NAP to show how much of its loss comes from inherited upstream splitters.

turns.user: ¿por qué se cae la señal cuando llueve?
turns.answer:
La documentación del proyecto (troubleshooting-guide.md) lo atribuye a la entrada de humedad:

- 
La humedad es una de las causas más comunes de un enlace que se degrada de forma intermitente en lugar de fallar del todo. La intrusión de agua en un cierre mal sellado o en una cubierta de fibra dañada hace que el revestimiento (cladding) de la fibra absorba parte de la luz transmitida, lo que aparece como atenuación que empeora durante o después de la lluvia y se recupera parcialmente cuando la sección afectada se seca.

- 
Un conector o una caja de empalme que no esté bien sellada es un punto de entrada habitual, y revisar juntas y sellos suele ser más productivo que volver a medir la fibra cuando la avería se correlaciona con el tiempo húmedo.

- 
Los cambios de temperatura pueden producir un patrón intermitente parecido al estresar mecánicamente un empalme o conector marginal, aunque el aumento de pérdida por ciclado térmico suele ser menor y menos brusco que el de la entrada de humedad.


Además, conviene recordar que 
la práctica es mantener un margen por encima del presupuesto de clase (habitualmente 3 a 5 dB), y un enlace con menos margen debería marcarse para revisión aunque hoy cierre el presupuesto
 — es decir, un enlace ya marginal es el primero en caerse cuando llueve.

Si quieres, puedo revisar qué NAPs o abonados de esta red están marginales y serían los candidatos más probables.

turns.user: What fiber attenuation value at 1490nm should I assume?
turns.answer:
I'll check both the documentation and the system's constants.
Two different figures exist here, and they disagree:

- **Documentation (gpon-link-budget.md):** 
fiber attenuation at the downstream wavelength (1490 nm) is commonly modeled at 0.22 dB per kilometer of route length for standard single-mode fiber in outside-plant conditions. Route length, not straight-line distance, is what this figure should be applied to — fiber follows ducts and poles, not a direct line between two points.

- **The system's constants:** 0.25 dB/km at 1490 nm downstream, marked industry-typical and pending validation.

So the value every optical budget in this network is actually computed with is **0.25 dB/km** (from the system's constants); the documentation's 0.22 dB/km is a different number and the two do not agree. If you are hand-checking a budget against tool output, use 0.25 dB/km; if you're following the written guidance, note the discrepancy and get it resolved, since neither figure has been validated against this plant.
